one_sentence: Healthy soil is alive. Tiny organisms help recycle nutrients, build soil structure, store carbon, and support resilient plants.

start_here.title: 1. Look up the soil
start_here.plain: Use the search box to look for soil names, clay, limestone, drainage, or habitat words.
start_here.why_it_matters: Different soils hold water, nutrients, and roots differently. Plant choices work better when they fit the soil.

start_here.title: 2. Read the benefit cards
start_here.plain: The cards translate microbial science into garden benefits like nutrient cycling, drought resilience, and healthier roots.
start_here.why_it_matters: You do not need to know microbe names to understand what healthy soil can do.

start_here.title: 3. Use it for better decisions
start_here.plain: Use the dashboard to ask: Is this soil shallow or deep? Clayey or rocky? Likely dry or moist? Better for prairie, woodland, or riparian plants?
start_here.why_it_matters: Matching plants and management to soil is usually better than trying to force the soil to behave differently.

start_here.title: 4. Know what this does not prove
start_here.plain: The microbial data are regional evidence, not a test of your exact yard.
start_here.why_it_matters: For exact fertilizer or soil-health decisions, use a soil test or local sample.

plain_terms.plain: Tiny living things in soil, including bacteria and fungi. Many are helpful, some are neutral, and a few can cause problems.
The process of turning dead leaves, roots, compost, and organic matter into nutrients plants can use.
A clue that microbes may have genes for certain jobs, like breaking down organic matter or cycling nitrogen. It does not prove the job is happening right now.
A nearby or similar ecosystem used as a comparison. It helps us make educated guesses, but it is not the same as testing your exact soil.
How sandy, silty, or clayey a soil is. Texture affects water, roots, nutrients, and drainage.
How acidic or alkaline soil is. Many Hill Country soils are alkaline because of limestone.
Dead plant material, compost, roots, and other carbon-rich material that feeds soil life and improves soil structure.

decision_cards.think_about: Use plants adapted to low soil depth, fast drainage, heat, and alkaline conditions. Avoid assuming more fertilizer is the solution.
Protect structure, avoid working it when wet, keep roots in the ground, and use plants that tolerate slower drainage.
Consider flood tolerance, deeper roots, erosion control, and organic matter protection.
Use soil texture, depth, and moisture clues to match native grasses, forbs, shrubs, and trees to the site.

safe_takeaway: Use the dashboard as a soil-and-benefit guide, not as a prescription. It helps you ask better questions before planting, amending, irrigating, or restoring.
